title: Showcase: something made up
summary: Two pieces for the family, one of them your own improvised loop, with names said and one question.
materials: the piece from your teacher, with a pencil

figure.alt: Two boxes stacked, one for the written piece and one for the improvised chord loop, the two pieces played in this recital, one of them made up rather than written down.

steps.title: A recital with something made up
steps.body:
Same shape as every recital: pieces played, names said, hands in frame, one question at the end. This time one of the two pieces is something you made up yourself: the chord loop and your improvised line over it.

1. Choose a written piece and settle on your favourite version of the improvised loop.
2. Run the written piece once a day, and practise the loop until your favourite line feels natural, not memorised word for word.
3. Say the slip plan out loud before you play: keep the beat, carry on from the next bar.
4. On recital day, say each name, calling the improvised one "my own piece," play both, hold the last note, and bow.
5. The family asks one question. Answer it, then write the Practice log.

Playing something nobody wrote down for you, in front of people, is a different kind of nerve than playing a page. It is worth noticing which one felt harder.

figure.alt: The same two boxes, the written piece and the improvised loop, each run or practised once a day before recital day.

steps.title: Recital checklist
steps.body: Tick each one before recital day.
checklist: Written piece chosen, and a favourite version of the improvised loop settled
Written piece run once a day, the loop practised until it feels natural
Slip plan said out loud: keep the beat, carry on from the next bar
Names said, including calling the improvised piece your own, then a bow
The family asked one question, and you answered it

steps.title: Record the recital
steps.prompt: Record both pieces in one take, names said out loud, phone where it sees the hands. Slips stay in.
